content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose an evaluation metric for feature attribution that compares the projection of the normalized attribution from a given technique on the all-one vector to that of sampled Shapley. The authors then show how the proposed metric has some properties like stability and trustworthiness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
While evaluation of explainability technique is an important and pertinent problem, I don’t think the proposal in the paper has convincing evidence that the metric is principled and useful. Here are my concerns.

1. The proposal is very straightforward — essentially for a subset of features S, if the technique is question has attribution A_i for i \in S, and A^*_i are the corresponding Shapley values, the proposed metric = |A/||A||.1 - A^*/||A^*||.1, where A and A^* are the |S| length attribution vectors for the technique in question and Shapley values respectively, and 1 is an all-one vector on length |S| normalized to unit length. This is then averaged over the dataset. While simplicity itself is nothing to be critical of, there’s no clear justification I can see for the specific definition since one can come up with many ways of quantifying the deviation between A and A^*. More importantly, the utility of such a metric is unclear to me and I don’t feel convinced by the results section which I will elaborate further.

2. The result section has a few parts, and I don’t understand how they reflect on the quality of the proposed metric. The first part looks at the “stability” of sampled Shapley which boils down to looking at the variance of sampled Shapley for different number of sampled paths. For some reason, the author propose a new way to quantify variability instead of just using something like the ratio of the variance to the mean. The take-home message for me was: with more samples, the quality of the approximation increases for sampled Shapley which seemed fairly obvious. Next, the paper compares the metric computed using sampled Shapley to exact Shapley, and as expected, the two are correlated. This is again a reflection on higher number of samples leads to a convergence of Sampled Shapley to exact. I can’t find the number of samples for this experiment for sampled Shapley computation. Next, the paper shows the metric for some datasets and attribution techniques, and since there’s no baseline metric (or ground truth by design), I am not sure what conclusions can be made. Lastly, subjective human ratings compare how human intuition for a technique’s output corresponded to the value of the proposed metric. With a sample size of 4, and no clear relationship, I don’t know what can be said about the generalizability or insights these results might actually provide.

3. The writing is fairly clear but verbose, spending a lot of time going over details without a clear tie-in to the theme. Definition of Shapley values, and the axioms it satisfies, development of eq. 2, assumption 1, Lemma 1, discussion of sampled Shapley, proposition 1 and so on seem superfluous. On the other hand, unique claims like partiality of the metric to Shapley value based techniques are pushed to the appendix where they are barely discussed (appendix D). Similarly, the discussion of limitations has been deferred to the appendix.

4. Minor: in proposition 1, there’s a missing variable in the definition of variance. The plots are hard to read (like Fig. 7).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clear, but low on quality and novelty. Should be reproducible when code is made available.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper considers an important problem but in my opinion, doesn’t do a great job of motivating the metric or providing sufficient evidence for its utility. In its current draft, I would not recommend the paper to be accepted at the venue.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper aims at measuring the objectiveness of the attribution values assigned to input variables by an explanation method. It puts forward the idea of using the bias of the attribution map, which is defined as the difference between the explanation and the unbiased estimation of the attribution map.

Experiments show that, over several sampling steps, the stability of the anchor value used by proposed method is higher than that of approximated Shapley values.
The reported results suggest that the proposed metric is a faithful estimator of the original pixel-wise bias.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
+ Complementary to existing work
+ Despite aiming an objective evaluation, it still considers the human intuition on its analysis.

Weaknesses
- Structure of the paper could be improved.
- Figures are too small
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
The structure of the paper could be improved. In more than one occasion through its content, every now and then, the paper reiterates on the weaknesses or issues of existing methods. This effectively breaks the flow of the content. Here it would desirable to have a specific section on the section focusing on these weaknesses and refraining from continuously reiterating on this aspect. 
In addition,Figures presented in the paper are too small and makes their analysis very difficult. Here it might be recommendable to select a subset and present them in a larger scale.

Quality
The proposed method is sound, however, the overall quality of the paper gets hindered by the clarity/presentation issues earlier described.

Novelty
The conduced analysis is, to the best of my knowledge, novel. 
It addresses two weaknesses of current methods. First, the assumed lack of attribution of non-relevant regions assumed by ground-truth based evaluations on synthetic datasets. Second, building on observations from existing work it makes a case on the variable effect of context variables that is ignored by ranked attribution evaluation protocols.

Reproducibility
Code of the paper is said to be released upon acceptance.
While not guaranteeing complete reproducibility, it is a step in the right direction.
content.summary_of_the_review:
On the strong side, the paper complements existing work on the field by addressing two specific weaknesses. In addition, I find positive the fact that, despite having the goal of proposing an objective assessment explanations, the human factor is still considered. Finally, the code used in the conducted analysis will be released.

On the weak side, the clarity/presentation of the paper could use some improvements (poor structure, figures too small to properly analyze). These aspects get on the way of the understanding of the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new way to evaluation attribution methods. In particular, it measures the bias of the attribution distribution, which is the difference between the Shapely value and the attribution value of a given subset of top-k-scored features. The evaluation is done on a wide range of methods and the CIFAR-10 and Pascal VOC 2012 dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

- Computing the Shapely value only for one coalition of top/least scored pixels is clever.
- A wide set of methods are studied in the evaluation.

**Weaknesses**:

- Missing limitations of IG and GI. See, Lundstrom et al. (2022 https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11912) for IG and Shan et al. (2021 https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12781) for the gradient.
- For Section 4: *"Besides, LRP-ε was not used on residual networks, because the relevance propagation rules of some structures in ResNet were not defined, to the best of our knowledge"*. This statement is not correct. There are rules for BatchNorm (Hui & Binder 2019 https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-20518-8_24), and the residual connection can be expressed as a linear layer. 
- **Which assumptions are used for approximating the Shapely values?** For approximating the Shapley values (equation 1), the paper cites (Ancona et al., 2019) which in turn is based on (Fatima et al., 2008). However, in (Fatima et al., 2008) a weighted voting game is studied, which seems to be a different problem than deep neural network. Unfortunately, (Ancona et al., 2019) does not discuss this difference. Please, document your exact assumptions for approximating the Shapely values. The whole approach could be questioned if the approximation is based on an invalid assumption. 
- The paper is a bit hard to read and the presentation quality needs to be improved; see next section. 
- In Section 5, the sentence, *"Although the proposed metric makes a breakthrough in the evaluation of attribution methods, it still has a few limitations.",* is too bold. Please, tone this sentence down significantly.

##
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** I found the paper hard to read. Especially, I found naming the difference to the Shapely values "bias of an attribution" confusing. 

**Quality:** Some figures are too tiny (Figures 5 & 7) to be readable without zooming, and in Figure 4, the text is badly overlayed on the actual figure. Please fix this.

Furthermore, I dislike that important parts of the paper are moved to the Appendix. Especially, Appendix J should be included in the main text. I would suggest shortening the subsection "Details about axioms and the Shapley value", as it only states general knowledge about the Shapely value. Similarly, I would also recommend discussing some limitations in conclusion (now included in Appendix J).

**Reproducibility:** The authors provided a detailed overview in Appendix I and promised to release their source code if accepted. 

**Novelty:** This exact evaluation was not done before.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this paper is currently not of sufficient quality and clarity to be accepted.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a evaluation metric of saliency map explanations based on assessing the explanation's conformity to Shapley value axioms. It proposed a method to estimate this conformity even though the exact Shapley values cannot be tractably computed. Experimental results reveal various findings about several existing saliency map methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

Evaluating the explanations in a quantitative and rigorous manner is an important problem. 

The paper writing, in particular on distinctions to other works, is generally clear and easy to follow. 

Weaknesses: 

My biggest issue of this paper is with the premise that Shapley value axioms should be taken as the ground truth. This manifests in several aspects: 

1. Shapley value axioms, like all other axioms, are intrinsically unjustifiable. Their utilities should be established with external validations (e.g. the explanations are useful for some purposes). For a concrete question, why should Shapley values, rather than integrated gradient axioms [1] be used? The latter also enjoy the advantage of being efficiently solvable (i.e. the IG explainer).  

2. There have been many evalutions based on model prediction under input perturbation according to the explanation. Examples include AoPC metric [2], deletion/insertion metric [3], and comprehensiveness/sufficiency [4]. How does the proposed evaluation compare with these metrics (which are generally quite similar to each other, differing mainly in minor implementational details)? If they are different, why should the reader accept Shapley value axioms as the correct one, rather than these (much more popular) alternatives? 

3. The authors spent a significant effort on refuting the series of ground truth based evaluations (Yang and Kim, 2019; Jasmijn et al, 2021, Yilun et al, 2022). By the way, it looks like the first and last names are switched in the last two references for some reason. They seem to provide a much cleaner and more controlled setup to understand model performance. Given that the proposed evaluation does not agree with the "ground truth", is it possible that the former is actually incorrect? This could be either because the Shapley axioms have undesirable effects, or because the implementation introduces error (e.g. removing pixels by graying them out (Fig. 4) leads to out of distribution inputs). 

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.01365

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06321

[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07421

[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03429

content.title: Evaluation of Attribution Explanations without Ground Truth
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes a metric to evaluate the objectiveness of  explanation methods without a need for the ground-truth explanations.
content.abstract: This paper proposes a metric to evaluate the objectiveness of explanation methods of neural networks, i.e., the accuracy of the estimated importance/attribution/saliency values of input variables. This is crucial for the development of explainable AI, but it also presents significant challenges. The core challenge is that people usually cannot obtain the ground-truth value of the attribution of each input variable. Thus, we design a metric to evaluate the objectiveness of the attribution map without ground truth. Our metric is used to evaluate eight benchmark methods of attribution explanations, which provides new insights into attribution methods. We will release the code when the paper is accepted.
